name: Halftime
about: Halftime is drum and bass at 170 BPM with the drums landing on half the beats, so the floor feels like 85 while the hi-hats, bass and edits keep full speed. Several threads fed it: the Autonomic experiments of dBridge and Instra:mental around 2009, Om Unit's and Fracture's footwork-speed hybrids, Amon Tobin's Two Fingers project and, decisively, Ivy Lab's switch from liquid funk to slow, sub-heavy beats in 2014, which gave the style a name and a label in 20/20 LDN. Alix Perez's 1985 Music, EPROM's circle and the Critical roster of Sam Binga, Chimpo and Fixate pulled it toward trap and dubstep weight. Halftime stays a producer's genre, strongest on EPs and in DJ sets, and its best albums are few.

artists.name: Ivy Lab
artists.why: named the style and built its label

artists.name: Alix Perez
artists.why: 1985 Music boss, liquid veteran turned halftime leader

artists.name: EPROM
artists.why: West Coast bass weight, Shades with Perez

artists.name: Mefjus
artists.why: neurofunk engineer who adopted the tempo

albums.title: FabricLive 50
albums.why: The Autonomic mix: half-speed drum and bass, electro and ambient blended into one grey, beautiful hour; the manifesto halftime grew from.

albums.title: Live for Never
albums.why: An Exit Records album of slow, synth-led drum and bass from the Autonomic circle, more mood than dancefloor and quietly ahead of its time.

albums.title: Nothing Is Certain
albums.why: NonPlus Records' first album, deep and pulseless where it needs to be; the ambient end of the Autonomic sound on a full-length.

albums.title: Resolution 653
albums.why: Boddika and Jon Convex's only album, cold electro and halved drum and bass with a sci-fi sheen; a NonPlus landmark.

albums.title: Mosaic Vol. 1
albums.why: Exit Records' compilation of dBridge, Instra:mental, Consequence and friends caught the Autonomic school at its peak and sketched the half-speed future.

albums.title: Stunt Rhythms
albums.why: Amon Tobin's alias strips his sound design down to huge, slow drums and bass; an instrumental rap-beat record that halftime producers quote constantly.

albums.title: Metahuman
albums.why: Rwina's West Coast producer at his most deranged, bass and glitch at half speed; the American weight that later entered halftime through Alix Perez.

albums.title: Chroma Chords
albums.why: The liquid funk star's second album slows down, darkens and adds vocal features; the pivot that made 1985 Music a halftime label.

albums.title: Threads
albums.why: Jim Coles's Civil Music debut braids footwork, jungle and halved drum and bass into warm, humane tracks; the style's most musical early album.

albums.title: Inversion
albums.why: A Metalheadz album that turns the Threads approach toward the dancefloor, heavier and more direct, with a Goldie-approved edge.

albums.title: Wasted Days
albums.why: Critical Music's first halftime-leaning album, grime and dancehall voices over snapping 170 drums; rough, fun and representative.

albums.title: Death Don't Always Taste Good
albums.why: The 20/20 LDN founders' debut album, trap weight and hip-hop swing at 170 with real tunes; the halftime record most people start with.

albums.title: Manifest
albums.why: The Austrian neurofunk engineer's second album spends much of its time at half speed, immaculately produced if emotionally cool.

albums.title: Infinite Falling Ground
albums.why: A looser, more psychedelic follow-up with chopped vocals and sampled haze; the style's most fully realised album to date.

note: Halftime's best work is on EPs and singles; these are its album-length records and the Autonomic precursors that frame it.
